-because you never once
touched on the budget, and you did not even tell us about your trip.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not like to make as lengthy speeches as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew).

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am very sorry that the weather was not better. I am not too critical personally, however, about your visit to the United States-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-because I learned something from your speech there that you had never said in parliament. It is always an advantage to hear cabinet ministers speaking in other places while parliament is in session, because they are speaking more freely than they would in their very responsible and dignified positions in this house. It does not help parliamentary responsibility, however, or aid in instructing the rest of the house.
The Budget-Mr. Rowe
I am not going to follow the defensive speeches of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) or the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I noticed that the longer the Minister of Justice talked the more involved he became, and the more he defended the more he had to defend. I quite realize the heat with which he crossed the floor, and I am glad that the language of the minister and the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) was not placed on the record, because when they are not on their feet they are both capable of describing each other. I do feel, however, that it is rather novel that the minister of defence should be on the defensive so much this afternoon.
I know that we have had the laughs and jeers of those who have been the yes men of this government, and who express such brilliant gibes when they are sitting down but express so little when they are standing up, no matter what is stolen or burnt. As the minister has said, I know that the loss is only a small portion of what we are spending-2 per cent or a half of one per cent. A million or two here or there: it just cannot be possible that it is disappearing. In fact, the Minister of Finance is always more sure that his budget is right if it is large enough. The larger it is the more he can boast about its greatness. The more burdensome it is on the people, the more certain he is that he needs the money.
I have read the budget, and I have listened with interest to some of the speeches that have been made. I have not heard them all, but judging from those I have heard from those who sit to your right behind the government, I am at least consoled by the fact that I did not miss very much in the ones I did not hear. I feel that the government seems to have given us a budget which the taxpayers of this country accept, Mr. Speaker, but it contains the highest taxation and is the largest budget this country has ever known. If it is conspicuous by its size, it is even more conspicuous by its vagueness and its lack of relationship to any fiscal policy. In fact, I have been waiting in vain to hear from the Minister of Finance, or his rather fluent assistant, any description of fiscal policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are so seldom here you would not hear it if we did give it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was here long before the hon. member, and I have been here long enough to know that if he were speaking every day I would not be here as often as I am, because I would not be missing very much. I have watched the hon. member since he came into the house. I know that he is so sure of himself that he likes to hear himself very

The Budget-Mr. Rowe often, and always did. But, Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that the noise a member makes is any indication of his contribution to this house. I have heard the hon. member many times, and he is becoming about as efficient as some of those who jibe when they are sitting down. He is generally good at that. However, as he progresses and attains a dignified role, he may live to learn that it does not pay.
I wish to Wring to the attention of this house the fact that we are carrying a burden which I think is dangerous. In bringing down his budget I must say that the Minister of Finance has almost become a magician. You have all seen the advertisement throughout the years for the old Magic baking powder.
I believe we might call this a kind of magic budget powder, because it convinces the taxpayer who does not look into the matter very much, except when he is making out his income tax form, that he is paying less than he was. The minister very clearly showed the people that their taxes were going to be reduced, yet through some magic formula he showed that our revenues are going to be higher. I have listened to many budgets, and to many ministers since the days of the Hon. Mr. Robb. I must give my congenial friend the Minister of Finance top marks and the grand championship for being able to take from the people with one hand, give to them with the other hand, and yet show them that they pay less while he receives more. I think it is very clever. My dear old friend the Hon. Mr. Robb, whom the present minister knew very well, was not a lawyer and so was never able to convince people as the present minister can that they were paying less but he was receiving more. However, Mr. Speaker, civil government and civil administration by the government, in a country the size of Canada, which is a growing country, is a great burden on our development. I refer to civil administration itself, the bare necessities that need to be paid for, in order to run the affairs of this dominion.
But there is something on top of that. There is not an hon. member in the house who does not realize and appreciate the tenseness of these times. They realize that we might be thrust into war at almost any moment and that suddenly, like a lightning flash in the night, our whole existence might be threatened. Independently of party, there is not an hon. member in this house who is not ready at all times to co-operate with the government and to try to help constructively in order to see that the money is properly spent and that preparedness for an awful day such as that which may come sooner than we think shall go full steam ahead and indeed

be the first obligation on the Canadian people. That is our duty to ourselves, to our people, to our country and to civilization itself.
The amounts that are mentioned are tremendous. To speak again of the days that I was referring to, this budget now before the house is eleven times larger than the budget which was introduced when I entered this house. It is just eleven times as large as that one. You are taking eleven times as much from the people. Despite the need for defence, the government has gone on and on with regard to expenditures. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) no doubt must have a new way for spending money on social security and the welfare state almost every time there is a cabinet meeting.
I see the Minister of Finance smiling. I will credit him with this virtue: he is not quite as wildly extravagant as are some of his colleagues. Nevertheless, he is not as careful as I should like to see him be. At a time when the defence obligations of this country are so essential and so vital to our very existence, surely we should at least be careful about superimposing upon those obligations other forms of obligation that may well-nigh threaten the economic progress of this country.
On top of all the defence obligations we have not only a social security or welfare state program but a debt reduction program and a surplus-provision program as well. The surplus last year was twice as great as was the whole budget in 1925. I am referring to the surplus alone. Mr. Speaker, I am not going to use just my own words, although I have had some experience in watching budgets and in trying to make a business pay. I have also had a lifetime's experience trying to make a farm pay, and I certainly have had the normal experiences in watching what makes progress possible.
Coming from that great city of Montreal, the Minister of Finance has watched business grow. I must credit him with knowing at least some of the essential and fundamental necessities in connection with keeping a business flourishing. He said:
X wish to emphasize however that we cannot have all these and reduce budgets too. Canada can afford these things we are doing but only at the cost of forgoing expansion or improvement somewhere else. Trying to do them all will only result in inflation. We must all hold some of our projects and programs in reserve even though they are sensible or indeed profitable.
What he is saying there is merely this. If we are going to do all the things some of his politically-minded colleagues would suggest, and are going to give everybody everything that is asked for, are going to give as many people as many things for nothing as they

wish at election time-if we are going to do all these things we are going to be in difficulty.
We must reduce other projects if we are going to spend more recklessly than ever before for civil administration. Never has a government spent as recklessly and wildly as has this government in connection with civil administration; never before has a government ventured in peacetime, or even in wartime, to spend so much on a defence program. Never before has a government ever ventured to spend so much on the welfare state. Never before has a government superimposed all these things, one upon the other, and ventured to have a surplus which is twice the size of some of our former budgets, and then planned to tell the people: We are reducing debt at the same time.
Mr. Speaker, not even a financial magician like the Minister of Finance can make that game last. When he tells you that he can do it only by retarding the economic progress of this country-when he makes that admission -it is time to stop, look and listen. The signals are out

and they are there in their tragic nakedness-warning us to view the future with great concern, if not alarm.
Mr. Speaker, the only way in which this country can ever afford to maintain the social services of the welfare state for which the pattern has been made is by an extension in industry and production such as we have never yet known. Even if there were a slight falling off, what would happen? The minister on another occasion said that he felt that we were in a very dangerous period when we had to tax industry 50 per cent of their net earnings or when we had to tax industry 50 per cent. He has made that statement on various occasions. Yet he now glibly tells us: We are going to take 54-6 per cent from the industries of this country. Where is expansion going to come if the minister is correct? From his long experience in his professional and civil life before he came into this house, he states exactly what is so true, namely that it can be done only at the expense of economic expansion.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the members of this house-those who are interested enough to be here this afternoon-will weigh that consideration seriously and ask themselves the question: Where do we go from here?
Mr. Speaker, it is true that we have been experiencing an all-time high in prosperity brought about by conditions and for reasons beyond the control of this government. Do not let anyone-even the most hard-boiled supporter of this government-think that the government has brought about this so-called
The Budget-Mr. Rowe prosperity or that they have made it possible for the Canadian dollar to be worth 2 per cent more than the United States dollar. This is a strong and powerful country. It has been said that some people are born to greatness, some achieve greatness and some have greatness thrust upon them. Canada as a nation has had greatness handed to her. Canada is a great country. It must be strong in order to stand a government as reckless as is the government we have had for the last few years.
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter that I wish to direct to the attention of the Minister of Finance. He smiles. I am glad that he can do so. That is one of the happy faculties he has. He can smile even in the face of possible tragedy, whether it be political or financial. And it is a good thing he can. Many people in Canada- will not be able to smile if he keeps on taxing them. I agree with him that he has no other course but to levy the taxes he is levying if he is to meet all the political obligations, you might call them, and all the things that will have popular appeal up and down the highways and byways of this country, because they must be paid for.
May I point out that today the textile industry is more or less in the doldrums and unemployment increasing; the leather industry is in a very serious condition today, and so is the lumber industry. That industry is threatened, and orders are falling off tremendously. I could add some others that the Minister of Finance knows very well are going to seriously affect his tax returns next year. He knows very well, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot continue to tax the people as we have been taxed, and expect this condition to grow better.
This government expects next year to take at least 30 per cent more from income than they took last year. Superimposed on that is a 2 per cent social security tax, amounting to an additional $214 million. It is pretty hard to see where there is any tax relief in sight and as these industries fail to pay the volume of taxes, there is little chance of the rate being reduced. However, I am aware that next year the government will likely try very hard to reduce taxation. Election year is always a great year for the taxpayer, and I am sure that the government will bend every effort next year to budget for a small surplus. In fact we will likely be told next year that a surplus is unnecessary, that a surplus increases extravagance and encourages spending. We will likely be told that we do not need to budget for a surplus. I can only say this in advance: The public will be waiting anxiously before an election is announced to hear the clarion call for an

The Budget-Mr. Rowe election; for next year's budget will tell whether there is to be an election or not. There has not been a budget by this government, or by the party that is now in power, in the last three elections in which they have not handed out hard-earned cash or reduced taxes or handed some form of bonus or a subsidy to get themselves reinstated because of the fear of losing power for the sake of power alone.
I said there is very little relationship between taxation, fiscal policy and the budget. Before I leave the taxes I do wish to say that I regret very much the minister did not see fit to allow deductions for hospitalization and medical expenses. I urge upon him that when the resolutions are up he reconsider it and allow the expenditures to be deductible before income taxes are paid.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is waiting for an election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As the hon. member for Greenwood has said, he is saving that as an election touch; in fact, it would be a very neat election idea, and along with that it would be very attractive. It would please the doctors, the nurses and the hospitals. It would please many people. If you cannot do it in any other way I urge you now to make that concession before the election, because the country needs it. I know that you allow any of us who wish to contribute to hospitals or to other charitable causes, to our churches and so on, to deduct those contributions from income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Up to 10 per cent of your income.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. Not many of us want to give much more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not many of us do.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. I leave it to the minister's own judgment to say whether deductions for medical expenses are not just as fair as charitable donations. If a person can afford to pay the medical expenses not of his dependents but of someone else's children, if he can afford to pay a thousand dollars, and some do, or five thousand dollars to a hospital for medical expenses, that ought to be deducted before income tax. If it were a charitable gift it would be deductible. Surely, if you want to pay $1,000 for the medical expenses of some crippled child, whether he belongs to your own family or not, it should be deductible from income tax just in the same way as $1,000 paid to a hospital drive is deductible. I compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on bringing this matter before

the house. I am glad that everybody supported it except the Minister of Finance. I am sorry that after receiving such support it was turned down toy the Minister of Finance. Again I urge upon him not to wait until an election year. Do it this year. There will be a lot of sickness this year. The minister is imposing heavier taxes on the people. Business is not as good as it was. There is a lot of unemployment. Many people need help this year. I plead with the minister again to reconsider and bring it in this year. As someone said to my right, better late than never. If you cannot bring it in this year, bring it in as an election sop, and it will still be good in 1953 or 1954, because if the government is defeated our party will carry out those good intentions.
I have been alarmed, Mr. Speaker, and I know the Minister of Finance has expressed his alarm, at what is going to happen to our business and to our expansion program that is so vital and necessary if this young country is to grow as it should. I am alarmed at the fact that there is no relationship between fiscal policy and this budget similar to what there should be and has been in other years.
It has been suggested that we should have a careful study made of our whole trade situation, especially international trade, and with that I am in full accord. I think you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that several years ago, and in fact on two or three different occasions, I urged that we should have an empire trade conference. It has been suggested very vigorously recently by our leader and by the hon. member for Lake Centre, but the government has paid very little attention to it. I would ask the Minister of Finance to reconsider that request. I believe every other party in the house has suggested that it would be bound to do some good. I recall the empire trade agreements of 1932. While these were difficult years, there is no one who remembers the proceedings of that conference who will not agree that the agreements were of great benefit to Canada at that time and for many years after.
At the present time the United Kingdom is studying where she can buy her goods, and we have given very little co-operation. In 1951 we purchased $31,900,000 worth of goods per month from the United Kingdom. At the present time, even though she is buying over $60 million worth per month from us, we have reduced our purchases from Britain by at least one-third, or approximately $10 million a month. On the other hand, the United Kingdom has sent her trade commissioners all over the world, and not long ago, when this great drive was

put on by red China and Russia, representatives of eighteen different countries visited Russia.
I believe Sir John Boyd Orr of Great Britain has within the last few months negotiated contracts to a value of $50 million with the countries behind the iron curtain. I have been wondering what is going to happen in this country. Great Britain is buying from us this year at a rate of $10 million per month less. It is now estimated that we will sell $70 million less of goods to Australia and to New Zealand than we sold last year.
Britain is buying lumber from countries behind the iron curtain; she is buying grain from the same countries; and she is trading her textiles to those countries, while our textile mills are closing. We have a situation which, if not dangerous, is certainly critical. But in the policies we hear from the government with respect to the expansion of trade we do not hear a word that would encourage enterprise. Indeed, in the words of the Minister of Finance, that expansion must be reduced.
The only expansion we see is in the welfare state. The only expansion to which the government adheres is that recommended by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who would spend all we make, and give even more away. So, if the government takes any credit for the kind of prosperity that has been thrust upon it, it must also admit that it has given very little opportunity for the development of any expansion program for the future.
Yes, it is truly said that the power to tax is the power to destroy. The government knows that now, if it did not know it before. I was amused when the Minister of Finance rose in his place and reduced the taxes he had increased at an earlier time on tobacco and cigarettes. And we will recall that there are reasons for his having done that. His reason for the reduction was that he had put the rate up so high that he collected a million dollars less in revenue. That, of course, is possible. I venture to say that if he raises the rates on personal and corporation income tax in the next year-and of course he will not do that, because it will be getting closer to an election;-he will have exactly the same condition, in general, as he had in connection with cigarettes and tobacco. The minister knows that in respect of those two commodities his revenues fell to the extent of a million dollars, because he increased the taxes to a point where sales dropped. That is possible in business.
I agree with the minister that when one gets above a 50 per cent tax on the business life of
The Budget-Mr. Rowe this country he is reaching the danger zone. That is why there are signs of curtailment and fears among the people who hold to the view that, by expansion and productivity, perhaps we could weather the storm of the future, no matter how severe it may be.
I am not going to speak at greater length. I would urge the government to reconsider some of its proposals, and to beware of the dangers ahead. There are many signs that are not good. I shall not do more than make a passing reference to the government's tendency to spend more because it knows it is going to have a big surplus. For instance, last year they spent about $17 million advertising themselves, about $4,500,000 on telephones and telegrams. In fact, they spent so fast that, when the surplus got too large, it was spent so that in the last few months before the budget it was half gone.
This year the minister says the surplus might be $9 million. But no one in this country knows what it will be-and, if one may judge by his record, the Minister of Finance does not know whether there will be a surplus of $9 million or $300 million, or a deficit. I venture to say however that if it is $300 million, instead of spending $17 million on publicity before an election, it may spend $34 million.
This is what creeps in when there are large surpluses. If there ever was a time both in business and in government when budgets were important, that time is now. They are important in family life, and as they apply to schools, churches and other enterprises. But they are vastly more important when related to our national business.
Every business in this country is taking stock today, and trying to economize all along the line. They are watching every dollar of expenditure for purposes of maintenance and repairs, and looking carefully at programs for expansion. I know of many industries that have reduced their expansion programs because they see danger signs. They see a tax of over 54-6 per cent on everything they make. They see increased interest rates, and they believe that with decreasing business it is time to take stock and to cut out extravagance.
Today our farmers are afraid of things in addition to the foot-and-mouth disease, because that disease has not done to the beef cattle industry much more harm than the sale of oleomargarine has done to the dairy industry. The importations of oils for oleomargarine have almost ruined the dairy industry, while the foot-and-mouth disease is threatening the beef industry.

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
Lack of fiscal policy on the part of the government has ruined several industries; yet we find among government members very little concern. We see extravagance in almost every department. This afternoon we have listened to three ministers defending themselves, arguing as to whether someone told them about a theft before a fire or after a fire, arguing whether it was started at one end of the building or at the other end, and admitting that it started in two different places-but no one knowing how much had been stolen in between the two fires.
We have today the spectacle of more civil
servants than were ever employed before, with
40.000	additional in the Department of National Defence alone-almost as many as there are soldiers. Those employees are falling over each other, and yet there were not enough left to patrol valuable property on New Year's eve. Is it any wonder that in some places nearly everything that was not nailed down was stolen?
Someone told me today-and I could scarcely believe it myself; and after the crossexamination between the 'hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) I am almost afraid to say what I heard; and I shall not give the names-but I was told that a skating rink was stolen from the defence department, including even the ice. Now, I can hardly believe that that could be true.
We do know however that millions of dollars' worth of equipment has been stolen from Petawawa. I want to know what these
40.000	civil servants are doing, now that they are on the payroll. Is one watching the other? As someone has pointed out, they have even stolen scales to weigh what they had stolen. Someone else says that they were sending telegrams to each other. It is bad enough to steal rolling stock; it is a bold thief who will tear up rails; but it is a bolder thief who will steal scales to weigh the scrap iron he has taken.
Well, that is the spectacle. These are burdensome figures. They arise from the taxation threatening to cripple industry in this country. They are coming from taxation that threatens to retard enterprise on the part of the individual. They are coming from taxation that threatens the very life of this country. And I say quite sincerely and seriously, even if it was the last thing I ever said in the house, that no matter what party is in power after the next election-and I have seen many changes; and I can hear the rumbling in the mulberry bushes even now-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are not making any forecasts, are you?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Forecasts are dangerous. I can hear the rumbling in the mulberry bushes now when you hear three ministers apologizing in one afternoon. You can hear it, and it comes awfully fast. It comes and hangs down around your ears before you know it is there. This government is powerful, but the larger they are the harder they fall. When they start tumbling they will fall over each other so fast in defeat that you will not be able to distinguish among them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You should know from experience.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have had some experience yourself. It is true that I have had more experience than my hon. friend, but at the same time they will fall so fast that you will not be able to distinguish among them the really bright one like the Minister of Finance and the duller ones who think more when they are sitting down than when they are up speaking. They will all look alike when the tide turns. I know it seems to be a fine thing to them to adopt the tactics they have adopted. The Minister of Finance is looking a lot older since he came down here.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Justice.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Finance looks younger every time he gives us one of his budgets. He looks even younger today than when he first came here. All these tactics do not disturb me. I think of Sir John Macdonald who said that you always find the most sticks under the best fruit trees. Whether it is the leader of the Social Credit group or the leader of the C.C.F. party that they start knocking and making those little chips of personality they will find that those persons grow larger and more influential all the time. The same game was played with one of the greatest statesmen this country has ever produced, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. I well remember the whispers of death and all the other games that were played. They tried to play the same game with that great leader Sir Robert Borden. They are trying to play the same game now with the leader of our party. They tried it before he became premier of Ontario, and then in three elections, which he won. They are trying to play the same game now.
It is all part of their tactics, wise or otherwise. I say that advisedly, without casting any reflection on anyone. I am not going to point out the ones who do it or who have devised the plan, but I do say that their tactics are becoming conspicuous to the public of this country. The respect which we pay

personally to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) of this country as leader of your party can be distinguished from the type of respect you pay to the great leader that we have, who I believe will be the next prime minister of this dominion.
On this side we are not at all ashamed, we are not at all disturbed because we know they are simply the old tactics. When the tide turns they will find that they have not worked. The public will then be looking for someone to replace the government who have fallen in spite of themselves. The government is growing weary. It is a government without a policy. It is a government which is carrying on extravagant and wasteful expenditures. It is a government which is trying to carry on five different avenues of expenditure at one time, like a juggler at the circus trying to keep five balls in the air.
The public will consider that it is time for a change. When it is time for a change they will not talk about some of the petty tactics that have been used or about what somebody said eight or ten years ago. They will ask whom they can get to replace the great Prime Minister whom we all respect as a gentleman. It is the same type of campaign that has been used in by-elections and general elections-they say that the Conservative party cannot form a cabinet.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear them saying, "hear, hear." God has been good to those wonderful men to your right, but surely he did not place all the ability in this country in the old Grit party. I think the Lord had better judgment than that. I know that that has been said many times before, but I know the people will look for a leader who has outstanding ability, who has unchallenged integrity, who knows where he is going, who is not afraid to fight or to lead. Our leader probably would be more popular if he were more fearful. He would probably be more popular if he told everybody everything they wanted to hear. He would probably be more popular if he would try to enlarge the welfare state and make it bigger than ever.

speechtext: I appreciate very much the fact that, after what I have said, the Minister of Justice is ready to say, "we want Rowe." I would not join your cabinet even if you did ask me. I must correct the Minister of Finance and tell him that I have not been carried away with my enthusiasm. Apparently they have been so carried away with my logic that the Minister of Justice is saying that he wants to hear more. I am not going to speak about my enthusiasm or logic, but I do want to say that I appreciate the courtesy that has been extended to me to continue. I appreciate the hearing that has been given to me by the few that are here.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On your own side too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to leave with the Minister of Finance a fair warning of the signs on the horizon. He should urge this government to do what any sound business enterprise must do today, count the cost and expand rather than retard your enterprise. The minister should send out his men to find what can be done to encourage industry to expand. I know that even my hon. friends to my left will agree that the only job security labour can have is by an expanded industrial productivity.
As the Minister of Finance has said, we cannot have that if you continue to tax and tax and tax. The power to tax is the power to destroy and to continue to tax as you are taxing now, while it may not destroy entirely, will retard; and then when times change, as they are changing in many industries, the crushing burden will fall, not only on that industry but on the welfare state. The two per cent will look pretty small with which to pay old age pensions when there is not much from which to take the two per cent. Things will be different when your income is shrinking. The old age pensioner should be aware of those political apostles who for the sake of power, and power alone, are ready to say, "We will give you twice as much again if you will only continue to vote for us." There are only so many shekels in the pot. Do not kill the goose that lays the golden egg because she is not laying as well as she was.

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon (Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 8, after lengthy and laboured compilations intended to explain the mistakes that he made in the budget estimates, the hon. minister stated that for the sixth consecutive year we have a surplus. Instead, in my opinion, he should have said that for the sixth consecutive year we tax our people more than is necessary. Such great revenue surpluses over expenses as have been piled up in 1951 by this regime, while municipalities and school boards must resort to provincial grants in order to meet their obligations because they are unable to make both ends meet, show clearly and definitely that the central power unfairly appropriates fiscal sources which do not belong to it.
For the government thus to pile up money surpluses when our workers are working their hearts out to make both ends meet is unthinkable, and it was only natural for our people to expect to be relieved of a substantial part of the tax burden.
Alas! the federal government is an ogre and it will relax its grip only to claw more strongly at the Canadian taxpayer. They assume all rights, assume responsibilities beyond their purview only to gain an electoral advantage by extending their paternalism to fields outside their jurisdiction.
Out of every dollar paid in taxes by the Canadian taxpayer 77 cents go into the coffers of the federal treasury. From 1945 to 1951 inclusive, the federal government has collected in taxes the amount of $9,988,624,394 of which $2,810,440,687 came from the province of Quebec.
Out of this amount, $4,810,343,705 were paid as income tax of which $1,212,530,887 were paid by my fellow citizens of Quebec.
It is not surprising, then, that provinces and municipalities, through lack of funds, should be unable to proceed to the development of any material projects which would improve living conditions of the community or make up for shortcomings in the social security program.
The unavowed aim of the Ottawa government is to reduce if it can the provinces to beggary and to bankruptcy, while depriving them of the revenue which they urgently require to achieve the task entrusted to them by the constitution.
In economic life, large corporations do not act differently. They begin by engaging in unbridled competition against their rivals.

Having reduced them to indigence or to an extremely perilous position, the large corporations supplant them by absorbing them. Thus we see the strong swallowing the weak. But should not things condemned in economic life also be considered reprehensible in politics and in national life, wonders that distinguished Montreal journalist, Leopold Richer.
Making use of his talents as a juggler, the Minister of Finance attempted to persuade the people that income tax would be lowered by 6 per cent, whereas the load of taxation will actually be heavier in 1952 than in 1951.
I do not like that way of doing things any more than I like the attitude of the Minister of National Revenue who announced as a gift the refunding of income tax to millions of taxpayers who had paid too much during the last fiscal year.
In doing so, the minister is not making gifts to anyone. He is simply refunding to the taxpayer part of the money to which he is entitled, money of which he was unfairly deprived on his pay cheque.
I say part of the money, because the government has had free use of the money for a certain period and refunds it without paying interest, while it demands a high rate of interest from those who owe it anything.
During fifty-two weeks the government takes away too much from the workman, the small wage earner and collects millions of dollars that do not belong to it, but when the time comes to return that money to its rightful owners, it adopts an attitude of liberality.
These are expensive refunds for the country. Considering the staff and the paper work needed in connection with that operation, the delays and the correspondence resulting from it, we find that the refunds made by the government bear heavily upon the population.
The request of the CTCC asking the federal authorities in the memorandum it has submitted this year to set the exemption from income tax at $1,500 for single people and at $3,000 for married people with a reduction of $400 for each child is reasonable and sensible.
Those who govern us must protect the family and allow all those who ensure the continuity of the race and consequently the strength and prosperity of our country to meet the appalling cost of their needs and to fulfil the obligations which they have towards their children. It is a factor which should not have been disregarded and which should be kept in mind while our next budget is being prepared.

The Minister of Finance would be well inspired besides to consider what help should be received by parents who direct their sons and their daughters towards our high schools and our universities where they receive the finishing touch to their education.
Every student who is 21 years old and who has no personal income should be classified as a dependent. But the government exerts more pressure than ever on the unfortunate father at the precise moment when his children's education becomes more expensive; as a result, many gifted and richly talented students are unable to complete their education and cannot enter the career they might otherwise have chosen.
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon ter, has cost our people, up to now, over $100 million not to mention the dead and wounded, and tortures of all kinds.
Our government is neglecting peace and the works of peace for the benefit of warlike ventures.
I cannot approve that policy and shall vote accordingly.

On section 1-Incorporation.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the specific task of the House of Commons at this time is to decide for or against the incorporation of Boundary Pipeline Corporation, whose sponsors are seeking the right to build a natural gas pipe line in southern Alberta as far east as Winnipeg. To arrive at a decision on this particular bill, parliament I believe must first make up its mind on a much broader and far more important issue; that is the issue of a national gas policy, the framework upon which the actual structure of pipe lines may be built and upon which to establish our attitude towards the Boundary Pipeline bill and the many other matters which will, over the years ahead, be a proper concern of parliament.
The purpose of a national gas policy may be summed up in these words: The mating of areas with proved and potential natural gas reserves to the market areas inside and outside Canada, subject to the marriages being economically sound, and the provisos that the matchmaking be planned to bring the maximum possible benefits to the areas of gas reserves, the Canadian gas consumers, and the Canadian economy as a whole. This involves getting gas to as many Canadians as possible.
An effective gas policy will help provide adequate incentives for continuing exploration to increase the nation's proved gas resources; an effective gas policy will also directly and favourably affect the rate of petroleum reserves discovered in Canada, the growth of petro-chemical and other industries based upon the by-products of gas and petroleum, and the growth of other industries within Canada that may use gas as a fuel.
At the present time the only province in Canada with gas reserves big enough to be wedded to outside markets is my home province of Alberta. Like many proud parents, my home province has been reluctant to recognize that its gas progeny are getting big enough and numerous enough to warrant marriage to some outside markets. Recently, however, Alberta approved what might be called the engagement of its Peace river gas reserves to the Pacific coast market. The coming marriage may be expected to set a precedent for others.
Before going on let me mention the great importance of the coal industry to the national economy in both peace and war. In view of *the fact that gas export will reduce to some degree markets for Canadian coal in areas now served, and the fact that national interest requires that the coal industry be maintained in a reasonable state of health, the government should take, coincident with

building a gas pipe line, all possible steps to expand marketing areas for Canadian coal, and speed research for new uses of coal.
I recognize the right of provinces producing natural gas to fully protect their own long-term supply from their own resources, and their right to determine the fields or areas from which gas may be exported, based upon surplus of reserves over local needs in such areas and/or the desirability of exporting dry gas in order to obtain valuable by-products contained in the raw or wet gas of certain fields. The Canadian government, however, has the right and the responsibility of determining the disposition of natural gas declared surplus of its own needs by any province. A national gas policy, if it is to serve Canada to the best advantage, must take into account a number of factors. First, it must recognize the right of provinces possessing gas reserves to reap a maximum possible benefit from them, and in so doing in a material degree determine route of pipe lines. Second, it must recognize the national interest which, in some circumstances, will mean supplying all gas to one section of the country rather than to another, or to some section of the United States instead of to some gas-hungry portion of Canada. Thirdly, it must recognize the economic facts of life-the relationships in distance and terrain between gas fields and prospective markets, both in Canada and the United States; the costs of getting, transporting and selling gas; competition with other fuels; the need of incentives to keep finding more gas reserves. Fourthly, it must recognize the political facts of life, which in some degree reshape economy both in Canada and in our neighbour to the south.
In the light of these facts there are certain guiding principles upon which parliament should grant incorporation to companies seeking the right to build interprovincial or international gas pipe lines, and upon which the board of transport commissioners, or some other appropriate body, should recommend to the government the granting of permits for the construction of such lines. Among these principles should be: a sound economic basis to support the pipe line; preference to be given to serving Canadian markets wherever feasible, construction on Canadian soil wherever feasible, of pipe lines between Canadian fields of origin and the most distant market to be served; construction on Canadian soil of a maximum possible mileage of a pipe line, if a portion or all of the gas is to serve a foreign market.
A national gas policy must recognize that export to the United States may be given
Boundary Pipeline Corporation favourable consideration under certain conditions. For example, there are United States markets essential to the economic operation of pipe lines to certain Canadian markets which are inadequate in themselves to support a pipe line project. We should not bar export in cases where exchange agreements could be made for an equal volume of United States gas to supply Canadian markets far distant from our own fields, provided the exchange is on a long-term basis, guaranteed at a lower cost than the gas from Canadian sources. Nor should we bar United States markets in the near vicinity of Canadian gas fields which, by reason of their location or type, do not economically fit into the Canadian supply picture. Nor should we bar United States markets whose serving with Canadian gas could provide very material Canadian national defence or economic benefits.
Another important phase of the national gas policy should be the ensuring of very material Canadian participation in pipe line projects. It is desirable that a substantial percentage of equity stock and bonds or debentures be made available for purchase by Canadian corporations and investors. Weight should be given to the degree of Canadian financial participation planned when the appropriate authorities consider each pipe line application. Weight should also be given to the extent of participation by pipe line sponsors in the exploration for and development of natural gas resources in Canada. In other words, are they seeking gas for all o part of the proposed pipe line's need?
Of Canada's provinces, only Alberta has the great majority of its urban population served with natural gas, and only Alberta has a growing surplus over and above its own long-term requirements. Its gas reserves are spread over a territory exceeding 120,000 square miles, stretching from the American border into the northern Peace river and Athabasca river regions, and stretching from British Columbia to Saskatchewan. The number of known gas areas in Alberta now exceeds 150, and the number is increasing at the average rate of one new discovery per week.
Northeastern British Columbia, adjoining Alberta's Peace river area to the west, became a promising gas area because of small discoveries a year or two ago. In recent months northeast British Columbia has come through with what looks like a major gas field in the Fort St. John area. This region, now separated from any large markets by hundreds of miles of small population territory, is taking on growing importance in the planning for pipe lines.

Boundary Pipeline Corporation
Western Pipe Lines Limited would build a line having, by its fifth year, an indicated market of some 70 billion cubic feet yearly, and increasing thereafter. Of that total about 154 billion-or 22 per cent-would service southern Saskatchewan and Manitoba cities as far east as Winnipeg. The other 55 billion cubic feet, or some 78 per cent of the total, would be delivered at the American border south of Winnipeg to Northern Natural Gas Company, for use in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. A contract has already been signed between Western and Northern for a year-round steady supply of about 150,000,000 cubic feet daily, this being subject of course to Western getting the right to construct a pipe line from Alberta. Northern is a United States firm already operating large scale gas transport and distributing pipe lines from the midcontinent United States as far north as Minneapolis. Western's plan is economically sound only if it gets the large United States outlet in addition to the market of the Canadian prairies, according to sponsors of the company.
There is a third proposal for a pipe line eastward from Alberta-that of Boundary Pipeline Corporation, whose bill for incorporation is now before this house. Its sponsors propose a 16-inch diameter pipe line from southeastern Alberta to Winnipeg, a much smaller scale project than either Trans-Canada or Western. I am opposed to the bill on several grounds. The Boundary pipe line project is condemned by its limited size, the very fact which its sponsors have ^presented as its virtue. Even if a small .[DOT]size pipe line from Alberta to Winnipeg [DOT]were an economic project-which I question
__the proposition falls far short of meeting
Canada's best interest because:
First, it would open up only a limited market for the rapidly growing gas reserves of the west. It would not, for example, open a market of sufficient volume to allow the Pincher Creek field and its by-product industries to develop on an economic basis. Small scale export eastward would not meet the increasingly urgent market need for Pincher and the host of other south and central Alberta gas fields.
Secondly, the Boundary project would penalize consumers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. A small scale line would have to sell gas at substantially higher prices than would a major project.
Thirdly, acceptance of the Boundary project could delay, perhaps for years, the securing ,of gas in large volume for Ontario and Quebec, either toy direct pipe line from the west, or by gas exchange with the United
States.
[Mr. Nickle.i
I question whether a line built to serve the cities and towns of southern Saskatchewan and Manitoba would be economic. In other words, I doubt whether it could serve a large enough market, or deliver gas at a low enough price to compete with other fuels, to obtain adequate revenue to recover its cost.
Eliminating Boundary, we would have two projects to choose between, both of large size that would open major markets for Alberta gas, and would deliver gas to southern Saskatchewan and Manitoba at lower cost than would a limited project like that proposed by Boundary. Which would best guarantee gas supplies to Ontario and Quebec, and bring the broadest benefit to Canada? The answer is not quite as simple as it might appear at first glance.
The all-Canadian route proposed by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines offers as its advantages: a major construction project all within the country; the only economic means of delivering gas to Canada's lakehead cities, and the potential mining and pulp and paper markets north of the great lakes; and possibly greater security of gas supply for the mass markets of southern Ontario and Quebec. The disadvantage of the Trans-Canada project is that the cost of gas to consumers in southern Ontario and Quebec would be somewhat higher than cost of gas that might reach these markets from the United States. These higher costs would stem from the comparatively limited markets en route to eastern Canada, the long distance, and the nature of terrain and climate that would make construction and operating costs higher than for a line from the mid-continent United States.
That brings us to the question: Can a supply of gas be obtained from the United States? Unless a long-term firm gas exchange can be worked out, it would be better for eastern Canada to have a guaranteed supply of gas from Alberta at higher cost than to have lower priced gas from the United States but no guarantee of continued supply.
Much has been said about gas exchange in recent years, and is continuing to be said, in the United States and Canada by sponsors of pipe lines and distributors of gas. I do not recall, however, any statements on this matter made by the governments of the two countries. There is a pressing need for a decision on this at government level, because within a comparatively short time Canada will likely have to choose between a Win-nipeg-Minneapolis and an all-Canada pipe line eastward from Alberta. There are also the facts that: (1) Alberta and Canada have already authorized, and have started, export of 10 billion cubic feet of gas yearly to

defence industries in Montana; (2) southern Ontario gas distributors are again seeking even short-term supplies of United States gas for their increasingly urgent needs; (3) in order to give Vancouver gas, Canada is seeking the right to export large volumes of gas to the United States Pacific northwest; and (4) the United States apparently desires Alberta gas for its atomic energy installations in Washington and Idaho.
In the light of these several facts, and in order that a sound national gas policy might be evolved, I suggest to the government that it immediately initiate negotiations with the government of the United States to determine whether or not a large-scale, long-term firm agreement is feasible for exchange of natural gas.
May I further suggest that, in order to facilitate the execution of a sound national gas policy, the government should immediately instruct Dr. George S. Hume and Alexis Ignatieff, geological survey of Canada authorities on our natural gas, to make a detailed re-survey of gas reserves, proved, probable and possible. Such a survey could probably be completed in three to four months. It would supplement the excellent, detailed reports on Alberta gas reserves, as of last December 31, prepared by the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board. The Hume-Ignatieff re-survey should cover, in addition to Alberta, the known and potential gas resources of northeast British Columbia, the Yukon and Northwest Territories, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Such a survey should be supplemented from time to time by revisions based on new gas discoveries, and further evalua:ion of fields already discovered. Such information would be of tremendous value in shaping the specific detail and carrying out of a national gas policy.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Chairman, we find this house giving consideration to a bill which would provide a charter for another company that wishes to build a pipe line in Canada. Before proceeding I must say that I was greatly interested in noting with what intent interest the members on the government side of the house listened to the hon. member for Calgary West when he was speaking just before I rose. At this point I might say that I think the committee is most fortunate to have a member who is as well informed as is the hon. member for Calgary West on the technical aspects of natural gas transportation and marketing.
This bill, Mr. Chairman, is entitled "An act to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation". Why are we getting this succession of bills to incorporate pipe line companies

Boundary Pipeline Corporation during the last two or three years? Why such interest in the transportation of Canadian natural gas? Why, on occasion, repeatedly in the committee and sometimes in the house, is there a suggestion that there is great haste to get the bills passed and to let the companies get the charters? I just want to read briefly from a report that I have here in my hand. I might say that one of the major witnesses for this company, when asked what the purpose of the company was, said that they were anxious to give service to the people of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I do not question the fact that if the pipe line were built they would give service in this respect to these people. But that is not their prime motive. Their prime motive is to be found in the fact that it is a profitable investment to get a charter to build a pipe line in Canada. I am not questioning the motive; it is a legitimate one as things are today. We must, however, realize that this American capital is being attracted to Canada because there are opportunities to make good profits

and guaranteed profits-in a public utility of this type.
I have in my hand the 27th annual report to the shareholders, 1951, of the International Utilities Corporation. I will just read two or three short paragraphs to indicate what valuable things these charters are and for which provision is made when the House of Commons passes a bill that gives a company the right to build a pipe line. Reading from page 3 of the report I find the following:
The past year was marked by many developments favourable to the long range outlook for our corporation and its subsidiaries in Alberta, Canada . . . The business of the subsidiaries for the year 1951 was again at record levels. Gross operating revenues increased nearly 16 per cent, $14,221,000. Despite substantially higher income taxes-*
I presume the Minister of Finance hears that.
-increased allowances for depreciation and higher operating costs, consolidated net income reached $1,700,000, an increase of $210,000 over 1950. In addition, net profit on the sale of investment securities amounted to $263,000.
Then again:
Consolidated net income was equal to $2.07 per share, exclusive of investment profits, and $2.39 per share, including investment profits, based on the average number of shares outstanding. This compares with $1.90 per share reported in 1950. Computed on the shares outstanding at the year-end, consolidated net income was equal to $1.80 per share excluding investment profits, and $2.08 per share including such profits.
We in this group, Mr. Chairman, have continually advocated and suggested that these private carriers of oil and gas should be publicly owned. We believe that the main transmission lines used for the transporting of oil and natural gas in this country should

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy be nationally owned, and that those nationally owned lines would sell the gas to the various companies concerned-and the same with oil -or would charge a fee for the transmission of gas or oil for the various companies using this service. If we had social ownership of the means of transportation through pipe lines of oil and natural gas in Canada today, I believe we would not have this unplanned competition for charters. We would not have applications being made for charters over the same route, or this duplication of charters, or this possibility to secure charters through the House of Commons and to sell them without building a foot of pipe line because of the right vested in the charter. In our opinion-that is, in the opinion of this group- if we had socially-owned pipe lines for the transmission of oil and gas in Canada we could plan the distribution of Canadian oil and Canadian gas in a proper and efficient manner, at possibly a lower cost to the consumer, without the duplication and the competition and, shall I say, the lack of planning that exists at the present time when company after company makes application for a charter over the same route, and sometimes conflicting with the legitimate interests of another company and so on.
I see that it is now nine o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to move that progress be reported.
