speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in an earlier speech in this debate I dealt with several features of the budget itself. Tonight I want to discuss housing. That is a phase of our economy for which the budget makes no provisions commensurate with the need existing today. The housing problem is today, as it has been for several years, our No. 1 domestic problem. With the single exception of national defence, there is no subject before this house that is of more vital importance to greater numbers of people than is that of housing. The need

is growing greater year by year. There are more than twice as many Canadians today without homes as there were in 1939. In that year the shortage was estimated at
225.000.	Today the shortage of houses is officially estimated at anywhere from 500,000 to 700,000. Only a few days ago the mayor of Windsor reported that more than 4,000 families in that city were not properly housed. At the same time we heard the mayor of Ottawa claiming that 4,000 families in this city were living in shelters that were below provincial housing standards. The Winnipeg city council special housing committee is reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 12 as saying that in that city today there is a permanent population of inadequately housed people. Since 1946 that city's housing committee has received 8,634 new applicants. The reapplications over these years total well over
20.000,	indicating that there are in that city many thousands who have been without homes for the last five or six years. A considerable number of applicants, the report states, are living in one-room slum dwellings with three or more children. Seven families, the report states, at the No. 3 wireless project are living in four rooms with seven or more children.
I had the occasion some months ago to visit the city of Brantford, the city that is represented by our highly esteemed Speaker in this house. That city is very prosperous, and in many respects a very beautiful industrial city. It is surrounded by some of the finest countryside we have in the province of Ontario. Yet here, out on the dilapidated airport just outside the city, hundreds of citizens with their families were crowded into what had once been barracks and other buildings used by the air force, crowded into small apartments with nothing but beaverboard partitions between them. The partitions were so thin that every sound that was made in one apartment could be heard through the walls in the other. There was no privacy. There were no playing fields for the children. When the soldiers occupied these buildings during world war II there was a well-kept playing field. There was a recreation centre; there was a swimming pool. When Brantford is obliged to use that as emergency shelter for the citizens there are no playing fields for the children. I saw puddles of water knee-deep out in front of some of the shelters. There was not a blade of grass to be seen anywhere there in midsummer. There was no swimming pool. The children were playing around the cement remains of what had once been a swimming pool for the air force. The conditions in Brantford could be duplicated in most of our larger cities and suburbs.

Anyone who has driven along No. 2 highway west of Toronto, through Mimico, through Long Branch, and has seen the trailer camps and has seen the emergency shelters out at Long Branch, will know that the conditions in Brantford, in Winnipeg and in Ottawa are duplicated in Toronto and elsewhere. Mr. McClaskey, regional supervisor for Ontario of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, told the Ontario association of real estate boards at Niagara Falls on February 19 that in his personal opinion Ontario alone needed today 450,000 housing units. Premier Frost stated in the Ontario legislature that for a number of years the province of Ontario will need 40,000 to 50,000 new homes each year if we are to begin to catch up with the demand for family accommodation. Mr. Earle Sheppard, president of the Ontario association of architects, stated to the council of that association, as reported in the Daily Commercial News for February 18, that the failure of house building to keep pace with industrial growth in Ontario was prejudicing the future of defence production. The value of contracts, awarded for factory construction, showed an increase last year over 1950 of 250 per cent, while the value of home building contracts showed a decline of 7 per cent.
He went on to say, according to the report:
It was absurd to concentrate on industrial construction and neglect the provision of housing for workers. Mr. Sheppard asked how can we get volume production of defence and other essential items if there are no places or only inadequate places for people to live? Every month hundreds of families move to or are formed in our great industrial centres. The time wasted in searching for accommodation and the worry caused by living in cramped unhealthy quarters result in reduced productivity. The housing shortage has plagued us ever since the end of the war, he said, and there is no sign of a concerted effort to solve it.
The Canadian Builder for March, 1952, has
this to say in an editorial:
Never has Canada's need for new housing units been so pressing as in 1951. There were about 150,000 marriages during 1951. Immigration stood at the highest point since before world war I, probably including 35,000 family units among the 170,000 newcomers. Natural increase of births over deaths was about 250,000.
This would seem to indicate that we could have done with at least 150,000 new family dwelling units last year. However, actual completions, according to dominion bureau of statistics figures were only in the nature of 80,000; starts were about 70,000; while total under construction at December 31 stood at around 50,000.
We have no right, Mr. Speaker, when we are today spending $2 billion to protect our way of life, to force tens of thousands of children, who will be our future citizens and probably soldiers in a future war or wars, to live in such ramshackle slums as they are living in today. I wish some of the cities and
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy boards of trade who invite members of parliament to visit their cities and large industrial concerns would take some of the cabinet ministers and some members of parliament through the emergency shelters in those cities and suburbs. I wish the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) could be taken on some of those trips. I am sure that the minister, full as he is of the milk of human kindness, once he became aware of the situation, would never sit idly by and see that situation grow worse from year to year. He must know that a few millions spent now on good housing would save his department many millions by way of medical bills and hospital bills in years to come.
. Mr. Sheppard said, in his report, that there is no concerted effort being made today to solve our housing problem. For six years since the war, now nearly seven years, governments at three levels in this country have all been playing a pass-the-buck game with our housing problem. They are still unable to reach any sort of agreement on the division of costs for building within the municipalities.
Housing has now become a national problem, a problem of grave national concern to provincial and municipal governments as well as to the federal government. One reason why there has been no concerted effort is that this Liberal government just cannot make up its mind where it is going, so far as housing is concerned. It cannot make up its mind whether it is getting into the housing business, or getting out of it.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) does not want the government to go into the landlord business, nor does he want it to go into the business of building subsidized low-rental housing. The explanation the Prime Minister gave the Trades and Labour Congress a few weeks ago was a unique one, one that is rather difficult to understand. According to press reports, the reason he gave is that there could not be enough of this type of housing to go round, and he said he did not like to see a system whereby any government or any political machine would have the selection of those who were to get houses.
It is rather difficult to follow the Prime Minister, or to understand what he means. Does he fear that eventually his successor to the leadership of the Liberal party will not be able to control political patronage within the party as well as he controls it at the present time? Or does he foresee a day when possibly some other party may come into power, and will be subjected to the lures of political patronage, more than is the Liberal government? What I suspect was his meaning is that today political patronage

The Budget- Mr. Noseworthy has become such an integral part of Liberal practice that the Prime Minister just cannot visualize a government housing authority that would select applicants for low-rental housing on any basis other than that of political patronage.
Even if we accept the Prime Minister's implied confession as genuine and realistic, and not an excuse for the government to keep out of subsidized low-rental housing, I would point out that the selection of tenants on the basis of political patronage could not be much worse than the system prevailing across this country today in connection with the allotting of government contracts and the appointment of government employees in connection with anything that comes under the authority of the government.
Under such a system, even with Liberal political patronage applied to the selection of houses, at least Liberals would get those houses. Probably they would get the new ones, and there would be some old ones left for the Conservatives and the C.C.F.'ers. Even that would be an improvement upon the present system.
Incidentally the Prime Minister is in excellent Liberal company when he takes this position regarding subsidized houses. In the latter part of March the Toronto metropolitan house builders association sent out what the press called a "ringing challenge" to all the speculating and contracting house builders in the greater Toronto area to get together and "to do something quick" to forestall the passage of proposed provincial legislation which would enlarge present assistance to subsidized rental housing. The national home builders association, according to the press statement, sent out a similar call to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, to the Canadian Manufacturers Association, to the Canadian Association of Real Estate Boards and to the Ontario Property Owners Association to oppose provincial legislation that could promote subsidized rental housing.
These are the people who agree with the Prime Minister when he says we do not want low-rental subsidized housing. Those of us who support subsidized low-rental housing also have some fairly respectable friends. Our friends may not be as affluent as those who support the Prime Minister, but nevertheless they are good and substantial citizens. For example we have the president of the government housing authority, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Mr. Mansur, in his address to the Winnipeg convention of the national home builders association, is reported in the daily press to have said that there is a definite need for
public rental housing in Canada. Then, the labour congresses in Canada have supported public rental housing for years-and I include the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour. In the briefs they presented to the government on March 26 and 27 both these organizations advocated subsidized low-rental housing as at least a partial answer to our housing problem.
A conference was called in Toronto early in March by the Ontario command (housing committee) of the Canadian Legion. It was comprised of representatives of welfare agencies, churches, labour and the construction industry. That conference passed a resolution proposing that the federal government pay subsidies to promote house building. Rev. W. W. Judd, general secretary of the council of social services for the Church of England, said at that conference:
The time has come when a further degree of subsidization is necessary. Housing is a social problem, not an individual one, it is the responsibility of the whole community.
In 1947 the Canadian Council of Churches took up the question of housing. This council is composed of all the Protestant churches in Canada and the following resolution was passed at that time:
The Canadian Council of Churches, believing that bad housing conditions are detrimental to healthy personal, moral and social life, and that public assistance is necessary to finance the building of homes for families with low incomes, urges the federal government to institute a national low rental housing program which will provide decent housing for low income families at rents they can afford to pay.
That was in 1947. At their annual meeting in Montreal in November, 1951, they passed the following resolution:
In the name of Christ, and for the sake of the health and morale of our people, we urge upon all levels of Canadian government, federal, provincial and municipal, the necessity and urgency of providing decent housing for people earning moderate or low wages and salaries, through an effective public housing program which will produce low cost and low rental dwelling units.
What is clear is that real estate boards and associations of speculative builders all support the position taken by the Prime Minister regarding subsidized housing. Trade unions, the Canadian Legion, the Canadian Council of Churches and responsible municipal and other officials concerned with housing do not support the government's reluctance tc provide low rental housing. On one occasion the Prime Minister is reported to have said that he did not want the government to become a landlord for a great number of citizens. The real estate boards and associations of speculative builders, along with the Prime Minister I presume, think that such a course would be socialism. I submit that

whether that be socialism or not, this government is already in the landlord business of necessity and against the wishes of the Prime Minister.
In 1951 the federal government was renting, mostly to second world war veterans, close to 25,000 houses. In that year they collected rentals amounting to $13,200,000. The government has found the rental business fairly prosperous. Of that 25,000 houses there were only 21 rental accounts more than three months in arrears and the total arrears amounted to only $413.
The reluctance of the Prime Minister and the government to go into the landlord business in compliance with the wishes of the real estate boards has had the effect of reduc ing the number of houses it has for rent. Last year, even with the 25,000 houses it has for rent, there were 14,000 fewer houses than in 1951. The government's policy of selling wartime houses which has been going on for a number of years, while not reducing the actual number of houses available, has made it increasingly difficult for many veterans who formerly occupied these houses to find accommodation.
I said that there has been no concerted action on the part of governments at the different levels, on the one hand, and on the part of the lending institutions, on the other. This is chiefly because the government does not know where it is going in the matter of housing. The government is torn between its allegiance to real estate boards, speculative builders, lending institutions, private enterprise and those who want to continue to build for the upper third income group, on the one hand, and the hundreds of thousands of those in the lower income brackets who six years after the war are still without housing.
The present situation constitutes a national emergency which is getting worse. Fewer houses were built in 1951 than in 1950. There is every indication that without some drastic change in government policy there will be fewer houses built in 1952 than there were in 1951. New housing starts to date are only 55 per cent of the 1950-51 level. The carryover on January 1, 1952, was only 46,000 as compared with 60,000 on January 1, 1951. The houses that are being built are being built for sale and for those in the upper third income group only.
Mr. Hignett, the regional supervisor of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of April 12 as saying that $3,300 is the minimum annual income required to maintain the payments on the lowest price houses being built in Canadian cities today, that is, four-roomed bungalows costing $8,500 with a monthly carrying charge of $63.50. He points out that 55704-117
The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy only those in the upper third income group today can afford to buy such houses. Today Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is serving only the upper third income group.
The condition is daily becoming worse. Building costs have increased 125 per cent since 1939, and during the same period wages increased 93 per cent. That is not all. Dr. Firestone of the Department of Trade and Commerce forecasts that building costs will advance another 20 per cent by 1955. This means that an increase of $10 in the monthly carrying charges will shut out of the home buying market all those with annual incomes below $3,500. It will shut off from assistance from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation those with incomes less than that amount. Any change which will reduce the monthly carrying charge by $10 will, on the other hand, bring many thousands back into the home purchasing field.
It is sometimes argued that the building of houses for those in the higher income groups provides vacant older houses which those in the lower income groups can move into. Apart altogether from the social stigma that would result from forcing those in the lower income groups into old houses, and even old houses would be better than none, there are a number of other factors. Old houses, like new houses, have greatly increased in price. Down payments on these houses are usually large and interest rates are usually high. There is no assistance provided by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the purchase of old houses. All these factors add up to a very grave situation for the houseless low wage earner.
I have said that housing is a social problem. If the hundreds of thousands living in cellars and garrets, in slums, trailers, emergency shelters and emergency makeshifts for houses are to be properly housed, we must adopt public policies that are not normally associated with an economically operated business activity. In other words, houses must be built and sold or rented at prices that bear some relation to the occupant's income regardless of whether or not that price will bring dividends in dollars and cents on the capital invested. There are values that accrue to a society of happy and contentedly housed people that can never be measured in dollars and cents. For one thing, a happy and contentedly housed people are one of our greatest offensive weapons against communism. I want to quote again what the Canadian Council of Churches has to say on this subject. On page 2 of their report there is the following:
Experience proves that emotional strains imposed on the crowded family group, major and minor delinquent behaviour among children when they stay away from home because of its discomforts,

The Budget-Mr. Noseworthy undermining of health through unsanitary housing conditions, and marriages delayed or dangerously strained by doubling up as a result of the housing shortage, all these produce conditions which are harmful to healthy personal and social life. The churches are convinced that the present housing shortage in Canada is one of the greatest single factors in contributing to shattered homes and families, and that the toll of broken homes and separated families will continue to mount unless immediate steps are taken to solve the low wage earner's housing problem.
Judge Allan Fraser of the Ottawa juvenile court claims that the housing shortage is "the greatest single factor" contributing to the breakdown in Canadian family life. In an address before the Ottawa Optimist Club, Judge Fraser said that he knew personally of housing conditions in the capital that were not fit for animals. "There are families of nine and ten trying to live in two rooms, with the father and mother sleeping on the floor," he said.
In Hamilton, Mayor Lloyd D. Jackson recently declared that "the story of housing in this city is absolutely heartbreaking. I can hardly begin to describe it." Miss E. Duffy, of the Hamilton Children's Aid Society, said that parents in increasng numbers were being forced to board their children out, and even part with them entirely because of their inability to get decent homes for them. "It is most important for the future of the children of Hamilton," she said, "that some remedy to the situation be found at once. Present conditions are contributing to child neglect, and our efforts to help parents improve their way of life are practically nullified by the seriousness of this housing emergency."
Just think for a moment of a country that can put $2 billion a year into the defence of our way of life, yet leave tens of thousands of children to be brought up in a way of life that is not becoming to a civilized democratic country! You may ask: What is the answer? There is no simple answer to that problem, as the minister in charge of this department well knows. I submit that first of all as a country, as a people and as a government we should recognize that housing is a social problem and that adequate housing will contribute values to society that cannot be measured in terms of interest or dividends on the money invested. I suggest in the second place that the minister and the cabinet should make up their collective mind as to where they are going in the matter of housing, whether the government is getting into or out of the housing business. If it is getting into the housing business, then subsidized low rental housing must be provided. I do not think that the Prime Minister's political patronage argument against it is a good reason for the government's refusal. More effective co-operation between governments at various levels is necessary to make section 35 of the National Housing Act operative.
If the government is going out of the housing business, if it is going to leave it to private enterprise to solve the problem, then the government must take such measures as will induce private enterprise to provide

society with an adequate building program. There are two difficulties that appear to have stood in the way of housing during the past year. The first one was the cost to the municipalities of providing serviced land and servicing the communities in which houses would be built. The second was lack of mortgage finance. When you consider that a housing program such as we carried out in 1949 and 1950, when we built about 90,000 houses, requires at least 25,000 acres of serviced land, you can realize the burden that is thrown upon the municipalities. Municipalities are loath to take advantage of the facilities of section 35 of the National Housing Act for the purchase and servicing of land for low rental housing.
The mayor of Windsor is reported to have said in the Ontario legislature that the present land assembly plan, under which the federal, provincial and municipal governments share the cost of acquiring and servicing land for building, is only scratching the surface and not meeting the real problem. Since every 500 new houses require a new school, municipalities are faced with additional costs for education. Numerous resolutions by organizations interested in housing have called for the federal and provincial governments to bear the full cost of education and social or welfare services within the municipalities. If it were possible for the federal government to provide relief by way of federal aid to education part of that difficulty would be removed. If the government were willing to get together with the provincial ministers of education to ascertain if some formula could not be worked out whereby this government may assure the provinces a part of the cost of education, the municipalities would then be able to devote more of their revenues to housing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I must inform the hon. member that his time has now expired.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget address was clearly and ably presented by its author the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It was vigorously criticized by the financial experts of the opposition, but they should not be reproached or feel too depressed if their criticisms made little impression upon this house or upon the public at large. Much time, I think perhaps too much time, has been spent in this discussion so I shall be brief.
The best indication of the soundness of a budget is the reaction of the taxpayers. Our taxpayers are a fairly intelligent lot. They realize that taxes form the great source of revenue for a government, and that if we are going to spend $2 billion on national defence,

a billion and a half on health and security and still find enough money to run the country, someone must pay taxes. They did not expect substantial tax reductions at this time. True, certain industries were suffering. They made representations to Ottawa during the year, and they obtained relief. When I was home at Easter I received calls from many people expressing appreciation for what had been done. In fact, I only received one letter of complaint from an individual in the civil service stating that he thought civil servants were the forgotten people, and asking me for an appointment to discuss their case when I next returned to Regina.
No one denies that taxes are high, but everyone realizes we are better able to pay taxes now than at any other time in our history. People believe also in the pay-as-you-go system. Never have people been better paid, better fed, better clothed and, may I say, better governed than they are in Canada today under this Liberal government. I was surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He and his associates generally claim to be the friend of the little man. But let them not forget there are some little men in business, and the little men in business needed this tax relief to protect their businesses and save them from bankruptcy. Let me suggest to him and his associates that they should ascertain the facts before they pass judgment.
I should like to discuss a matter of great importance. Almost a year ago a royal commission was appointed to study the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project. It consisted of Dr. T. G. Hogg of Toronto, chairman; Mr. G. A. Gaherty, Calgary; and Dr. John A. Widtsoe, Salt Lake City, Utah; and Mr. B. T. Richardson, Ottawa, secretary. Here is the order in council under which they were appointed, and here are the terms of reference. The commission was to conduct an inquiry into the following matters, namely, whether the economic and social returns to Canada and to the Canadian people on the investment in the proposed South Saskatchewan river project would be commensurate with the cost thereof, and whether the said project represents the most profitable and desirable use which could be made of the physical resources involved. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the inquiry is on the South Saskatchewan river project and the possibility of building a safe dam in a proper location and the economic soundness of the proposed irrigation and power project.
There is a sixth paragraph in the order, by whom it was suggested I do not know, but it tends to make this direction ambiguous 55704-U7i
The Budget-Mr. McCusker and leave it entirely to the commission to determine its terms of reference. This project has been studied and reported upon for fifteen years. Under the direction of the Department of Agriculture, men of the staff of the P.F.R.A. have studied and prepared reports on every phase of this project. I should like to put some of their names on the record. They are: Dr. L. B. Thomson, director, P.F.R.A.; Dr. C. C. Spence, senior economist, dominion Department of Agriculture, Edmonton; Mr. G. L. MacKenzie, chief engineer, P.F.R.A.; Mr. G. M. Munro, assistant chief engineer, P.F.R.A.; Mr. A. E. Palmer, superintendent, dominion experimental station, Lethbridge; Mr. G. W. Parkinson, chief of design section, P.F.R.A.; Mr. J. G. Watson, construction engineer, P.F.R.A.; Mr. R. Peterson, soils mechanic and materials engineer, P.F.R.A.; and Dr. J. D. A. Mollard, engineering geologist, P.F.R.A.
In addition, they had as consultants such eminent engineers as Major General H. B. Ferguson, Washington, D.C.; Dr. A. Casa-grande, Harvard university, Cambridge, Massachusetts; Mr. L. F. Harza, construction engineer, Harza Engineering Company, Chicago; Dr. J. A. Widtsoe, irrigation and soils expert, Salt Lake City, Utah. They had two eminent contracting engineers-D. S. MacDonald and W. B. Ramsay-as consultants. Mr. Speaker, on my desk are reports upon the work done and recommendations made by these men. These reports are all available to the commission.
The commission met in Washington a few weeks ago where all these men and many others were available for consultation. They were in western Canada last year and they are there now consulting the governments of the three prairie provinces. Why they should waste time consulting governments whose views are already well known is beyond me. It is well known that a royal commission should deliberate very carefully before bringing down a report, but in this case all the evidence has been accumulated and presented to them so the process of arriving at a conclusion should not be a lengthy one. I would earnestly ask the government, therefore, to modify the terms of reference if necessary to see that a report on this project is made in the very near future. When this report is made, if it be the desire of the government that the commission report on other things I shall have no objection to their sitting longer.
After the remarks made by the Prime Minister today I was inclined to eliminate this portion of my address, but later in the

The Budget-Mr. McCusker day I saw a statement made by Mr. Richardson, the secretary of the royal commission, as it appeared in the Regina Leader of April 26. The article states:
He said public hearings in Saskatchewan were being planned tor the "near future."
The Saskatchewan hearings will be held after the commission has examined the mass of engineering and technical data it has assembled.
It is expected the commission will make its report this year.
Well, gentlemen, I think we should not delay much longer in getting a report. Mr. Speaker, at a time when we are spending four and a half billion dollars per year we cannot hesitate for a moment to develop our natural resources wherever we may find them. It is only through the aggressive development of these natural resources that we can ever hope to meet our ever-increasing expenditures.
Since I have been in this house I have been watching-I am glad to see the member for Rosetown-Biggar and I hope he will come in and sit down along with the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). I am glad to see them here because I wish to discuss the C.C.F. tonight. In Ottawa, the C.C.F. appear mostly as a group of benign individuals exuding honesty and benevolence. In Saskatchewan, where they form the government, they appear in their real character, and may I say a not very attractive character. During the Easter recess I spent a few days in Vancouver, British Columbia. The C.C.F. of British Columbia were in convention, and announced their platform for the forthcoming election. Under the leadership of Mr. Winch and son, they decided to go "full out" for nationalization.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No provincial election speeches.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Giving away other people's money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hydroelectric, mining, lumber, pulp and paper, fishing-all industries were to be nationalized. Hospitalization, although very expensive in British Columbia today, was to be given at a much reduced rate and medical care was to be entirely free. One must give them credit for boldly telling of their intentions. Their intentions are similar to those of the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan when they first came into power. In fact, Mr. Fines, the financial expert of the C.C.F., was in British Columbia at that time. Was he there in an advisory capacity or was his visit purely a coincidence?

When the C.C.F. came into power under Hon. Mr. Douglas in Saskatchewan, they proceeded with their program of nationalization. What has been the result?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Failure.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The people must like it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Transportation is a monopoly and should have been a profitable one. Their capital was given to them by the government. They had no interest charges to pay. Yet they have made no money.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly they made money.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let him make his speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not seen this year's statement but last year the only part of that system which made money was the lunch counter in the bus station in Regina.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The company had an over-all
profit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then as to the box factory in Prince Albert, Mr. Mitchell, the owner had trouble with his men. They struck. The government told him that unless he settled immediately they would expropriate the property. He said: Do that. They did. What resulted? It is failure.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was not failure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The fish filleting plant has practically ruined the fishing industry in northern Saskatchewan. As to the lumber business I will not repeat what the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) said. He covered that situation some time ago and explained what a mess they have made of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is doing very well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As to the sodium sulphate plant, they sank $1 million into that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the production of that plant?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They had to close it down last fall and call upon their competitors, v horn they had tried to put out of business by making them pay high royalties, for assistance in filling their contracts. Then what about the woollen mill in Moose Jaw? The hon. member ought to know about that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It employed 125 people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Financially it is a failure. The tannery was a failure and was closed down. As to the shoe factory, this was a good investment. They brought in an expert to run it and after they closed it down I asked him why. He said: I will tell you. It

should have prospered. It is a good little plant. I am experienced in that business but they gave me so many superintendents and sales managers that they ran the business into the ground. They advertised it for sale. The advertisement read: "A flrst-class opportunity for an experienced person." They sold it.
Then comes the insurance company. They initiated a cheap packet coverage for cars- one the line companies had difficulty to compete with. They lost heavily in that venture.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The lowest insurance rates in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but the company is practically broke as a result.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must not forget the brickyard because I have been named in Saskatchewan as being involved in that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you some shares in it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I happened to be president of International Clay Products. When I was overseas they told my solicitor that we would sell the plant to them or they would expropriate it. My solicitors went ahead with the other officers of the company and effected the sale to them at a very reasonable price. Since that time they have put half a million dollars into it. Last year, a little over a year ago, I went west. I was driving west alone and I met Mr. Sykes of the Journal. He said: I have a two weeks holiday. I asked: How would you like to accompany me out west? He said: Fine. As we drove out through Estevan we stopped to see this old brick plant. I hardly knew it. It was modernized. Half a million dollars should modernize a plant. I said: How many bricks are you making a day now? The answer was: 56,000. In the old days, with the old obsolescent machinery we used to turn out approximately 100,000. I said: How many men do you employ? The answer was: 96. We employed 80. I said: How is it that with 96 men, and all this modern machinery, you are making about half the bricks we used to turn out in a day? He said: It takes a lot of men to run those labour-saving devices.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are two public utilities listed here which were established in the old days by a Liberal government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They were always losing money in those days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are the telephone and power corporation. They were alone and
The Budget-Mr. McCusker set aside and managed separately from the other crown corporations until the picture painted of the crown corporations was so bad that they decided to link them up. Now when you say: How are the crown corporations doing, they say: "Fine"; and that is what I wanted to tell you about. They are being financed with profits made from the telephone and the power company, profits that should be used to extend power lines and to extend the facilities of the telephone company.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You just sit down for a moment. I am going to deal with you shortly. Time does not permit me to dwell at any length upon this formidable list of failures. What has resulted from that? Private enterprise was driven from the province. When the C.C.F. came into power in Saskatchewan Imperial Oil had five drilling rigs and seis-mographic crews working in Saskatchewan seeking oil. On account of the confiscatory legislation that was envisaged, they pulled out and went to Alberta and those crews are responsible for the discovery of Leduc, Red-water and three other major fields. It would have been rather nice to have those discoveries made in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much oil was discovered under the Liberals in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Finally, becoming alarmed at the loss of population in Saskatchewan compared to the other provinces, and impressed by the developments taking place in Alberta and Manitoba under free enterprise, the C.C.F. decided to drop the nationalization program and to attempt to bring capital to the province. They promised the oil company the same deal they were getting in Alberta.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you object to that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not at all. I think it is excellent. Just wait. Do not be impatient. You will hear the rest of it. They promised the oil companies the same deal as they were receiving in Alberta. The big companies swarmed in, seeking leases, for it is felt that the potential oil and gas resources of Saskatchewan are equal to those of Alberta. What happened? Instead of allowing the legitimate oil companies to bid for the choice leases, they gave a concession of 9 million acres to a Mr. X of Montreal. He paid one-tenth of a cent an acre for the lease. He was not a legitimate operator. He disposed of his acreage to the legitimate companies, who had been trying to get them

The Budget-Mr. McCusker before, at a handsome cash profit and retained a royalty of 2h per cent on 9 million acres. Here comes the joker. The C.C.F. government claimed they did not know this gentleman, that he was a perfect stranger. Yet he walks in and gets 9 million acres and goes away with a 2-J per cent royalty on them. I asked this question, as do the people of Saskatchewan: Who are his hidden associates? Dr. Schumiatcher, Q.C., then legal adviser to the premier of Saskatchewan and the government, formed several companies and applied for leases. He left the government employment on the eve of having those leases granted; they were leases amounting to hundreds of thousands of acres of oil land and a large acreage, 250 square miles, of uranium leases in the most favoured portion of Saskatchewan. Who are his associates? Now, gentlemen, you may get some idea of what is going on there with a C.C.F. government in power when I tell you this. During the short session of the Saskatchewan legislature a little over a year ago the government slipped through an amendment to the assembly act, which permitted members of the legislature to obtain leases of oil and mineral lands from the government. In fact I am told it went further; a member could hold leases through an agent, and that agent did not have to make known the names of those for whom he was acting. The storm of public opinion rose so high over this that the Saskatchewan government hastened to repeal the legislation at the last session of the legislature. A measure of comedy was added to this particular type of proceedings when the provincial treasurer, the Hon. Mr. Fines, produced and tabled affidavits to the effect that all the C.C.F. members of the legislature were honest men.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Soon we see a company formed with Mr. Bodnoff, one of Mr. Douglas's constituents from Weyburn, as president, Mr. Douglas and Mr. Fines as shareholders and directors and Mr. Schumiatcher as secretary-treasurer, to build a theatre under the stars, the Sunset Drive-in. Of course it was purely a coincidence that Mr. Bodnoff received a very large loan of $75,000 from the Saskatchewan government insurance company a short time previous to the formation of the theatre company. We all know now that the Saskatchewan government insurance company

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, there is nothing

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Liberals in a hurry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We all know that the Saskatchewan government insurance company comes under the department of the provincial treasurer, Mr. Fines. When he was asked

in the Saskatchewan legislature why this money was not placed in farm loans Mr. Fines is reported to have stated that they did not yield a high enough rate of interest, and so it goes on. The virus of private enterprise, once it got into their blood, spread just as rapidly and has been just as persistent as that of foot-and-mouth disease.
Another cabinet minister has gone into the hotel business. I want to read an editorial. Hon. members are objecting that I was giving too much attention to Saskatchewan. I will come right into this house. This is from the Leader-Post and is an editorial of April 28, headed "C.C.F. inconsistency", and reads as follows:
Redistribution should not be the "business" of parliament, nor of a parliamentary committee, Mr. Stanley Knowles, C.C.F. member for Winnipeg North Centre-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I understand that the question of redistribution has been referred to a committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is redistribution in
Saskatchewan that I am talking about, Mr. Speaker. I will not read the first paragraph which has to do with the statement of Mr. Knowles, and is no doubt the official view of the socialist party. The next paragraphs set out how redistribution is carried out in this house and I shall not refer to it. But since the rest applies to Saskatchewan I would like to read it, sir, with your permission:
Aside from the merits of Mr. Knowles' proposal, a point of interest to Saskatchewan is the wide gulf between C.C.F. talk in Ottawa and C.C.F. action in Regina.
Saskatchewan under the C.C.F. government had a redistribution a year ago, in preparation for the forthcoming election. Was it handled by an independent commission? The answer is "no." Was it handled by a committee of members, with representation thereon from both sides of the house? Again, the answer is "no." The only members who had anything to do with it were C.C.F.'ers, behind closed doors where the boundaries were drawn under the eagle eye of provincial treasurer Fines. Eventually, Mr. Fines, on behalf of the government, told the legislature where the boundaries of the constituencies were to go, and that is where they went, except for a few minor changes.
The Saskatchewan opposition did not go as far as to request an "independent commission" such as the federal C.C.F.'ers talk about. It moved an amendment to the redistribution bill asking that the present Ottawa procedure be followed, that instead of the government presenting redistribution as a fait accompli a special select committee of the house be established to redraw the boundaries with both sides of the house represented thereon.
I will not read the whole editorial. It was refused. This is what happened:
Saskatchewan polls that went Liberal in 1948 were lopped off here, and others which gave the C.C.F. a majority were added there to strengthen the shaky seats. Robert Walker, who won Hanley with a 51 majority in 1948, was fixed up with a majority of 166 if the people vote again as they
The Budget-Mr. McCusker
did in 1948. Shellbrook's boundaries were shifted to raise the C.C.F. majority from 175 in 1948 to a potential 388. Touchwood was lifted from an actual C.C.F. majority of 168 in 1948 to a potential 413 in 1952, or whenever the election is held. Kerrobert-Kindersley's potential C.C.F. majority was raised from 178 to 436.
And so it goes on. I just wanted to show you, Mr. Speaker, that performance is a little bit different from talk. The reason we have lost population is that we have a government which has brought -about a lack of industrial and business opportunity; a government which has passed farm security legislation which has made it impossible for our young men to obtain a loan to buy a farm; a government which prefers to use the people's money to develop movie theatres rather than to develop agriculture.
I should like the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar to state which, if either, of these groups he supports, the radical group o-n the coast or the capitalistic group in Regina. I am amazed that he can support either. Is he trying to walk a tigh-t rope between them? Obviously he should disown one or the other, or both.
I hate to mention the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, whose independent stand in this house last week sent a convulsive shudder down the spine of the leader of the C.C.F.-a tremour which was recorded in the press throughout Canada. This reaction, of course, amazed all hon. members of this house who had heard the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) attack the Liberal members, on the radio and in this chamber, for their honourable conduct towards their leader who, by the way, has never in any way attempted to interfere with our duties and privileges as members and who, moreover, never expects Liberal members to have their speeches vetted by him before they deliver them.
What happened to the poor member for Moose Jaw? He was summoned to the whipping post and emerged from that ordeal so thoroughly shaken that he was heard to mutter as he walked back to his room- "Mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa". He then dashed off an iron curtain confession of guilt and a new profession of faith. But what an ordeal that must have been for the usually loquacious gentleman who now sits in his room or in his seat in this chamber, in gloomy silence. In fact, tonight I have been one of the first to cheer him back a little bit towards normalcy.
Can it be that the leader of the C.C.F., seeing the Saskatchewan trend and seeing the free enterpriser in the bench behind him becoming bolder, feared a contest for leadership?

The Budget-Mr. J. O. Gour

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the farsighted budget he has laid before us. Every Canadian should congratulate the minister and also every member of the cabinet for having given the country such good administration and having shown a sixth consecutive surplus; thus they have reduced the national debt by $2,544 million, which means a saving of more than $62 million in interest charges for the Canadian people.
No, the minister need not be ashamed of showing such a wonderful surplus and I challenge our opponents to criticize it with worthy arguments to support them. As a matter of fact it is a government's duty, in time of peace and prosperity, to show a surplus in order to reduce the huge debts we have had to make, while we were forced to defend our country and civilization in order to ensure security to our fellow countrymen.
This year, the hon. minister has done even better for we have a surplus in a year that is, at it were, a semi-war year since more than $1,441 million was spent for our armies in Korea and elsewhere, again to provide for the security and the defence of this country and other countries which also want to defend liberty against the threat of communism.
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of piling up surpluses in peacetime and during periods of prosperity like the one we now enjoy in this country because we were compelled to run the country into debt to the amount of $2 to $3 billion each year in wartime. Should we again be compelled by our enemy to defend our country we would be in a better financial position.
If we are now enjoying great prosperity it is mostly due to the sound administration of the Liberal government as opposed to the administration we had between 1930 and 1935, during which period a Tory government directed the country's business until it was gotten rid of at the general election of 1935. What a good thing that was for everybody!
The people of Canada were then experiencing the worst industrial stagnation in its history, most of the workers being unemployed and many farmers and businessmen having gone bankrupt. These people were not then complaining about taxation, because they were not earning enough money to take care of their own needs.
The picture is altogether different today when Canada has undergone a thorough transformation; as a matter of fact, most of our towns and rural areas have improved out of all recognition. Consequently, I say that we should continue to proceed along the lines of good government and harbour no worry.
However, I find, like anyone else, that a budget amounting to $4 billion and a half represents a tremendous expenditure for a population of 14 million people scattered as it is over ten different provinces and the large spaces of a country such as ours.
With the permission of the house, I will review the reasons compelling our government to impose such high taxation. First of all let us see what conditions are in other countries in order to find out if we are paying more or less taxes than the people of these other countries.
Let us see, in the first place, how our friends from the United States fare. This country, with a population of over 150 million people, is one of the most advanced and the richest in all kinds of raw materials. Furthermore, due to its geographical situation, this country is able to grow all the products it requires. Its clever and resourceful people pay, on the whole, much higher taxes than our own. In spite of this, the United States have shown a large deficit for many years.
I now wish to quote from the New York Herald Tribune:
A New York paper praises Canadian taxation policy.
The New York Herald Tribune states, in an editorial, that Canada's answer to the threat of inflation places that country ahead of the United States on the road to secure stability.
In pointing out a few taxation adjustments announced last week in the Canadian budget, the newspaper adds that the people responsible for the preparation of the taxation program in the United States could take note of Canadian methods.
The willingness of the Canadian people to accept the bad news of a level of taxation high enough to offset an expanded budget is proof that they realize the fact that a taxation program which contributes to economic stability is an adequate program.
It is not by accident that since the war the Canadian dollar has reached parity with the American dollar, that the public debt of Canada has been reduced, that the American investments in Canada have greatly increased and healthier economic conditions than in the United States have been maintained.
Canada did not merely stick to a payment in cash policy. Having accepted the gross burden of taxation required to balance its budget, Canada has centred its attention on improving the efficiency and fairness of its taxation.
I challenge our opponents to say that they are not proud to realize that their Canadian money is worth more than any other money in the world, and that foreign capital is flow-

ing into Canada. Therefore, were it not for these governmental restrictions, we would get thousands of requests from citizens of other countries who would like to settle in Canada. While I am dealing with immigration, and though I am not opposed to it, far from it,
I would nevertheless like to suggest to the government that we should not proceed with too much haste in this connection, for I cannot see how we could receive more than 100 thousand emigrants a year, which, added to the natural increase of our Canadian population, would bring it up by 200 or 300 thousand a year. We must be logical and give these people employment.
But let us return to the reasons for levying taxes for an amount of $4 billion and a half. First there is an amount of $2,100 million for the defence of our country and for assisting less favoured people. I do understand that the amount is quite high for a population of 14 million. I hope that the threat to peace will subside and that we shall soon be in a position to reduce our armament program.
But what did our opponents say, and more particularly the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew), leader of the opposition? At the time of the invasion in Korea, in June, 1950, we were accused of not spending enough, we were told that we should be spending two or three times as much, that we were endangering the security of the country. Several members of the opposition even asserted in the house and at public meetings that we should have more than 200,000 men under arms and that we should resort immediately to conscription. Some of them went so far as to say that we should be a member of the Atlantic pact. To hear them speak, one would think that there should foe Canadians on guard duty all around the world. Really, Mr. Speaker, if the government were to listen to everything that is said by the leader and the Tory members, they would believe that the expenditure should not be $2,100 million but much more than $3 billion for defence alone. Our armed forces would comprise not a mere 100,000 men but 250,000 or even 300,000.
While I am speaking of the armed forces, I think it would be a mistake to accelerate the tempo of enlistments. We must, of course, fulfil our commitments, but we must also avoid subscribing to new obligations. It is a good thing to furnish war equipment, food and so forth; but it seems to me that
The Budget-Mr. J. O. Gour it would be still a better policy to draw the line as far as the sending of soldiers abroad is concerned.
Those countries have a right to expect our help and besides, by helping them, we actually protect ourselves; but let it be admitted that their population is ten times as high as ours, that they are at home and that their supply of raw materials is insufficient to employ their population. And while we open our doors to some of their youth, most of whom are of the same age as our young soldiers, our own young men are fighting on the battlefields. That is why I repeat, Mr. Speaker, it is all very well and also quite natural to help but we must not send more soldiers than we have now, except in the case where the danger should become greater.
I would not forgive myself if I did not refute the criticisms directed against us by the opposition and, for the most part, by the second and third oppositions and by many members who pretend to be independent but are greater Tories than the Tories themselves on the amount we are compelled to spend for the administration of the country, in addition to defence expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, I have made what I consider a fairly accurate calculation of what the amount would be if the government were to agree to all the expenditures they suggest. We would need a budget of more than six billion. Oh, how generous are our friends of the opposition! They are always prepared to suggest increases of all kinds, pensions, better wages for government employees, subsidies here and subsidies there, subsidies for everybody. If the water level rises and overflows in the springtime, in some little creek, the government should carry it away to some other place. To hear them tell it, one would think the government was a huge mountain of gold and that the only thing to do is to help oneself.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. members who endorse the policy of the Liberal government are as generous and sympathetic as the hon. members of the opposition when it comes to helping others, to making contributions out of their own pockets, and I challenge our opponents to find a single Liberal member who is not in favour of all social measures intended to help people of slender means, to give adequate salaries to the civil servants, to help our farmers through subsidies, our workers, etc., as well as foster education. We want adequate pay for our servicemen, we take care of our returned soldiers, we help our hospitals, we give fair treatment and an adequate salary to our workers, in

The Budget-Mr. J. O. Gour short, we promote by all possible means the development of our country and make sure that all Canadians will be treated justly so that our national unity will be preserved. But-and there is a "but" which we must not forget-all social laws ever adopted in this country have been sponsored by a Liberal administration. Every dollar spent by the government must be repaid by the Canadian people. That is why it is necessary to collect taxes and that is why we must not go faster than our resources will allow us to go.
And then after requesting that over $6 billion be given, contributed and spent, they turn around and accuse us of overtaxing the people. I understand that the role of the opposition consists in criticizing. Now, my good friends, be serious. During the Korean invasion, you had a fair game and you said that the danger was impending. Any man who is close to danger is ready to take any means, like during a thunder-storm we fear the thunder, and as we are good fellows we implore the protection of Divine Providence. Unfortunately, too often after the storm we forget to give thanks, yet sometimes people die without sufficient preparation. It is the same as far as the Korean war is concerned. Because things look a little better now, some are bound to forget and to blame us for too much preparation and, for the rest of the budget, we are blamed again after having been asked to spend twice as much or three or four times as much.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that no single member of this house who is a supporter of the Liberal government welcomes high taxation more than anyone else. To begin with, we also pay taxes, as well as our opponents and our friends who have elected us, not to mention those who have given their voice to our opponents. Most of the hon. members in this house wish to be re-elected with a greater majority. Then we must make new friends and keep such friends as we had before. Consequently, we want our families where the head of the family has many dependents to be taxed less, to receive a bigger family allowance, certainly less taxation for everybody, a pension for the disabled as soon as possible, an increased old age pension, etc., etc. But, where shall we find the money and yet incur no deficit? It is true that we have a surplus but that is a good investment for all Canadians. To support this contention I quote an article which appeared in the London Times: (Text):
I have a newspaper article headed, "Financial Strength of Canada Helping Buttress

Free World". It is dated April 15, quotes the London Times, and reads as follows:
The financial strength of Canada is helping to buttress the entire free world, the London Times says today. "Clearly Canada Is exceptionally favoured by fortune; but prosperity as well as adversity is a test of statesmanship, and much credit is due to Mr. St. Laurent's government for the happy condition of the nation's affairs," the Times says. "Canada may be congratulated the more wholeheartedly by her friends because her financial strength helps to buttress the entire free world."
(Translation):
To be able to enjoy prosperity, the finances of the country at least must be in good condition. In case of war we would be in a better position to defend our country and if peace should continue, as it is our wish, and if the markets where we sell our products become less profitable, our country will have to be in a sound financial position to undertake in due time vast projects to help the development of our natural resources and to ensure employment for our workers.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding I wish to ask the Minister of Agriculture who is not in his seat at the moment, but who will certainly read this request, to consider closely the prices of our farm products, because during the last few months the prices of cheese, beef, pork, eggs, poultry and milch cows went down by more than 25 per cent. Even now the price of the hide of a month or month-and-a-half old milk-fed calf is only 40 cents. We must remember that that requires an hour and a half of work by the farmer to skin a calf and that children's shoes sell at $2 to $4 and shoes for grown-ups sell at $10 to $15, which means first of all . . .
(Text):
If I may say it in English-fifteen hours of work for a farmer and ten calf skins for a pair of child's shoes...
(Translation):
. . . and forty-five hours of work and thirty calf hides for adults. Obviously, there is something wrong with our shoe manufacturers. I have investigated the matter personally and I was told that they have lowered the prices of hides and shoes considerably, but that they have increased wages. I think that they too need a wider margin of profit. Which means that at the present time our farmers are producing at cost, since there has been practically no reduction in the price of what they have to buy. Almost everywhere we see wage increases, which makes them think that the price of goods they have to buy will go up, since inevitably, when an industry increases its wages, it also increases the price of its products propor-

tionately. The railways and all the other means of transportation are charging exorbitant rates on all freight. So our farmers are leaving their farms. Statistics are there to prove it. That is why there is a shortage of housing in our cities. Such a condition can throw our economy out of balance and cause unemployment, and even a certain lack of balance in our society.
Agricultural loans are inadequate in Ontario. The provincial government actually neglects the Ontario farmer. The loans should be increased by at least 50 per cent. Instead of lending $4,000 on a farm, we should lend $6,000. It would be much easier then for the head of a family to purchase farms on his sons' behalf, for one needs more than $12,000 to buy the farm, the cattle and the necessary machinery. Such an improvement in the law would encourage farmers' sons to remain on the land, which would be an excellent thing for all Canadians.
I would feel remiss in my duty if I failed to remind our excellent minister of national health to see to it that bilingual old age pension cheques be distributed throughout Canada. I feel sure that there is not one of us who would not be in favour of unity and justice at home.
(Text):
I am of the opinion that there is not an hon. member who is not in favour of unity, good understanding and justice in this country.
(Translation):
We are descended from two great races with a glorious past. In this land of our ancestors, we speak French and English and we have been living in harmony for centuries; have we not become allies in several wars, standing together in the defence of freedom? Why should Canadians not be able to live side by side and respect one another?
To achieve that end, we must be treated equally well. Then let us have bilingual cheques, like bilingual currency. School legislation, although it comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces, should be applied without any discrimination as to race or language, and not as in British Columbia. This also holds true as far as religion is concerned. That would be in the greatest interest of Canada. Let us follow the example set by our young men, either French or English-speaking, who have shed their blood and made the supreme sacrifice at the front to defend their country, their race and their religion. We, who represent them all, should
The Budget-Mr. Gillis not fear to pass legislation accordingly and endow this country with a distinctively Canadian flag.
I conclude by asking Divine Providence to protect the health of our Prime Minister, who is widely known as a man of superior qualities and a great Christian.
