subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ordinarily I would only speak on the subject of the budget once, but sitting in the house listening to the speeches made, one begins to feel like a steam boiler. Since you have not got a safety valve, when you get up to a certain pressure the only way to relieve it is to say something about the things that are bothering you. I should like to say two things about the speech made tonight by the member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker). I am sure he would not want to mislead the house or make an inaccurate statement.
Tonight the hon. member used the figure of one and a half billion dollars as the contribution made by the federal government in the field of social security. I am sure that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare knows that figure is not correct. When he uses that figure of one and a half billion dollars he is including the provincial government's contribution, the money spent by the municipalities in the field of health and welfare as well as private contributions that are allocated for that purpose. I want to correct the record on that, and I am sure the parliamentary assistant would want me to do so. The federal government is not spending one and a half billion dollars; that is the total amount of money that goes into that field in Canada from the agencies that I have mentioned. The second thing I should like to put on the record is the position of the small industry in Saskatchewan operated by the Saskatchewan government. Now, it is not my prerogative to defend the Saskatchewan government in this house. There are five members from that province who are capable of doing that. The reason I am interested in the industrial set-up is that in my last election that was the only issue in the campaign in my riding, based on a statement made in the house by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenfoaker) just before adjournment. The Saskatchewan industrial set-up was a complete washout so far as the hon. member was concerned. Fortunately, I had just returned from Saskatchewan where I had spent two weeks, much of it in Regina with the men who were

The Budget-Mr. Gillis responsible for setting up and maintaining these small industries. I had the facts and figures in my pocket at the time the member for Lake Centre made that speech.
Immediately following the hon. member's speech I rose and put the facts and figures I had obtained from the men in Saskatchewan on the record. I have kept in touch with that industry ever since. If the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare will look at the budget speech made by the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan in 1952, he will find that in the over-all operation of industry under the management of the provincial government there was a net profit of $3'5 million. Those are the figures the provincial treasurer gave the legislature.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. member, but will he permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wanted to ask him through you, Mr. Speaker, if he included in that the telephone company and the power corporation?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was all-inclusive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the statement which I made. I think I said that the crown corporations standing alone did not carry themselves but they had lumped in with them, for the purpose of accounting, the telephone company and power corporation which were old corporations making large profits, and therefore it showed as though the whole scheme of crown corporations were making a profit; in fact the latter two concealed the actual deficits of the first.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not going to argue about the details. What I am interested in is this. At the time the Saskatchewan government took over the power operations in that province it was a dead loss, and the telephone company was in the same position. I am sure the hon. member will agree with me that the position of industry in that province at that time was nil. If I belonged to that province, regardless of politics, I would have to give the government credit for taking the initiative and trying to set up small industry on the prairies to create employment. There has been a wide expansion of power in that province since the government took over. 1 believe it is all to the good. I wish that the Nova Scotia government, with the resources it has available, would undertake a similar development. Regardless of the fact that it is a Liberal government, I would be one of the first to pitch in and help.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And New Brunswick too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the province of New Brunswick also. I merely say that because I am interested in the Saskatchewan government's efforts to put some industries on the prairies; that has never been attempted before. Of course these men were inexperienced and were feeling their way. Nevertheless, there are a lot of people who have employment in these little industries today, regardless of whether the money was made in power, in telephones or in the over-all picture. Some sections will lose.
For instance, take the Dominion Steel and Coal, a huge free enterprise octopus that stretches across this country. It has twenty-six subsidiary organizations, and you will find that many of those subsidiaries are losing money while others are making money. The over-all picture enables that huge organization to remain solvent, and in a position to employ thousands of people. I compliment the Saskatchewan government on that particular matter for creating employment and experimenting with industry. The men lacked experience, but I think they have made a very great success of it. I just wanted to straighten out the record on those two points.
There is another matter, Mr. Speaker, that I should like to develop rather fully and that is the question of whether there will be another fall session. The recriminations that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has to take, the accusations that the house is being prolonged for the purpose of giving members another indemnity-one hears those things. So far as I am concerned, as one member of this house, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that those accusations are justified. On June 8, 1951, I spoke on this question and pointed out that, so far as I was concerned, a second session was necessary, and I put the legislation that still remained untouched on the record. That prediction in June turned out to be correct because hon. members were here in December. They had a two-day recess for Christmas, and the business was not completed then, or not as it should have been.
Today is the 65th day of this session. If the session prorogued tonight, hon. members could go home and draw their full indemnities. What does that mean? It means that in the years gone by the anticipated length of the session was 65 days, and hon. members could complete their business when they were dealing only with the problems of Canada with 8 million or 9 million people. They did not then have the problems of the world to contend with as we have today. Anyone who takes a look at that order paper which I have in my hand-and I refer to today's order paper-and looks over the 34 items of legislation that are still on it, to

say nothing about the legislation that is yet to be brought forward in this session, such as amendments to the Criminal Code, the Combines Investigation Act, with regard to immigration, unemployment insurance, and all those things that will have to be dealt with-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And all the estimates.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and who thinks that that agenda can be completed by the end of June, is not figuring on giving that legislation much consideration. Then you have all of the estimates to handle in addition to the legislation that is on the order paper and the other items that we know must be brought in. In the light of all that, I am obliged to rise and say something about it. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has been fair, considerate and understanding as far as the members of the house are concerned. In addition to that, he wants to give everybody in this house an opportunity of examining that legislation, and not just rushing it through at the last minute.
On the question of remuneration, I want to compliment the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) who got to his feet here last evening and made a strong speech on that subject. When you take a look at the legislatures, for example, what do you find? I have in my hand a clipping-and it is dated May 1-which shows that in the province of N wfoundland the members of the legislature increased the indemnity to $3,000 a year. In the province of Ontario I think the indemnity is about $3,900. I think $3,000 is fairly well the indemnity across the country. In its last session the Ontario legislature sat for less than seven weeks. You must consider the fact that members of parliament come here from all over this country, many of them with businesses, many of them with law offices. You are not able to work here. Premier Frost recently made the statement that he figures that being a member of the Ontario legislature is a full-time job and that it is not possible to carry on as they have in the past and just consider it a part-time job.
As I said in June last year, we have arrived at the position in this country when members of parliament are going to have to make up their minds whether they are going to work for the people of Canada and accept the responsibilities that have been given them as members of parliament or whether they are going to stay home and look after their practice, if they are lawyers, their businesses if they are businessmen or their farms if they are farmers in some other part of the country. They just cannot do a good job either here
The Budget-Mr. Gillis or at home having regard to the time that must be spent in this parliament at the present time.
I am saying that because I think that the criticism and the kicking around that the Prime Minister has taken in the last few days is completely unjustified. I do not think he merits it, and I think it is up to the individual members of this parliament to show that they appreciate the fact that he has some understanding of and consideration for them, both with respect to the time they must spend in the house and as to the inadequacy of their compensation.
I think the time has come in this country when the government of Canada and the members of this House of Commons must do something. I do not believe in just putting the gun to the cabinet and saying: You must do it. As a member of this House of Commons I think I have some responsibility in the matter and should be prepared to express my opinion on it. I think it is a full-time job. I think the members of this House of Commons should be paid an adequate indemnity so that they might be able to do the kind of job that the people who elected them expect them to do.
I have in my hand the set-up in the United States as it affects our opposite numbers in that country. I am just going to put it on the record:
Beginning in January, 1947, the compensation of senators, representatives in congress, delegates from the territories and the resident commissioner from Puerto Rico is at the rate of $12,500 per annum each; and the compensation of the speaker of the house of representatives and the vice-president of the United States is at the rate of $20,000 per annum each. Whenever there is no vice-president, the president of the senate for the time being is entitled to the compensation provided by law for the vice-president. Starting also in January, 1947, each member of either house receives an additional $2,500 per annum as an expense allowance for which no accounting is made. Beginning at the same time the government contributes to an annuity which a retiring member of congress may receive after six years of service and attainment of the age of 62 years, or upon retirement for disability after five years of service.
I should like to ask hon. members of this house if they think that a member of the House of Commons who has to spend the amount of time that we have to spend in Ottawa doing the business of the country is not as good a representative or is not performing just as good a job as is his opposite number in the United States? Do you think the people of Canada, with regard to what their members should receive, are any more parsimonious than are the people of the United States? I do not think so. In this house I have stated a good many times that, as to the riding I represent, the only question I have ever been asked on the subject of

The Budget-Mr. Gillis remuneration is: How do you get by on it? How do you manage it in Ottawa for six, seven, eight or nine months of the year, maintain a family in this part of the country, and get by on the amount of money that you get?
There is no question as to what the member of parliament should be entitled to. I think the situation is the same in every riding of this country, if the member of parliament faced up to his responsibility and tried to have the people that he represents see the parliamentary job as it is today, under circumstances that have drastically changed over the last ten years.
I see that it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Gillis the debate was adjourned.
